blocks.text: 1. Batch Size
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445204155-509589687.png

Batches, the previous topic, introduced smaller groups of examples processed one at a time. Batch Size is the specific hyperparameter controlling how many examples go into each batch, already covered in general terms there.

It is a single number with genuinely far-reaching practical consequences, touching gradient stability, training speed, memory usage, and even generalization, all covered in full depth throughout this topic.
2. The Effect Of A Small Batch Size

blocks.alt: The Effect Of A Small Batch Size
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445204155-869919540.png
This connects back to Stochastic Gradient Descent's own noisy updates, already covered in its own topic. A genuinely small batch size, closer to that extreme, produces noisier gradient estimates.

It also produces genuinely more frequent weight updates per epoch, since more, smaller batches fit within the same dataset, a direct tradeoff already covered conceptually as Batches' own middle ground in the previous topic.
3. The Effect Of A Large Batch Size

blocks.alt: The Effect Of A Large Batch Size
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445204156-177655273.png
This connects back to Batch Gradient Descent's own stable updates, already covered in its own topic. A genuinely large batch size, closer to that extreme, produces more stable gradient estimates.

It also produces genuinely fewer, more expensive updates per epoch, since fewer, larger batches fit within the same dataset, the direct opposite tradeoff from the small batch size already covered in the previous section.

blocks.text: 4. The Genuine Memory Constraint
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445204509-33341644.png

A genuinely real, practical hardware limit governs batch size choices too. Every example in a batch must fit in memory simultaneously during the forward and backward pass, already covered throughout the Backpropagation & Optimization module.
Genuinely larger batch sizes require genuinely more memory, a real, practical ceiling that often determines the largest batch size a given piece of hardware can actually support.
5. A Genuinely Counterintuitive Generalization Effect
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445204510-71677472.png

A genuinely important, somewhat counterintuitive empirical finding follows. This connects back to Batch Normalization's own regularization side effect, already covered in the Normalization Techniques module.

Genuinely smaller batch sizes can sometimes generalize better, thanks partly to this same noise already covered there, since the added variability between batches can act as a mild, implicit form of regularization.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This generalization effect is empirical and not universal. It genuinely depends on the dataset, architecture, and other hyperparameters, and should be verified through actual experimentation rather than assumed automatically.

blocks.text: 6. The Coupling With Learning Rate
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445204511-215292594.png

This connects back to the learning rate, already covered throughout Gradient Descent. Batch size and learning rate genuinely interact with each other, rather than acting as two fully independent hyperparameters.

A genuinely larger batch size often calls for a genuinely larger learning rate to compensate, since more stable, averaged gradients, already covered in this topic, can typically tolerate a bigger step without becoming unstable.
7. The Common Powers-Of-Two Convention
A genuinely common, real practical convention chooses batch sizes as powers of 2, like 32, 64, or 128, rather than arbitrary round numbers like 100 or 50.

This genuinely aligns well with how modern hardware, like Graphics Processing Units, processes data efficiently, since their internal memory and computation structures are commonly organized around powers of 2.

blocks.text: 8. Batch Size Versus Dataset Size

This connects back to Epochs, already covered in the previous topic. Batch size, together with dataset size, directly determines how many batches, and updates, fit in one epoch, already covered conceptually in that topic.

This is a genuinely direct, concrete link between this topic and the previous one, since dividing the dataset size by the batch size gives the exact number of updates that will occur within each single epoch.
9. Recognizing How To Choose A Reasonable Batch Size

blocks.alt: Recognizing How To Choose A Reasonable Batch Size
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785445204511-232259884.png
Genuinely limited hardware memory is a direct case where a genuinely smaller batch size, already covered, becomes a practical necessity, since a larger one simply might not fit at all.

Wanting genuinely stable, reproducible training with ample hardware available is another genuine case where a genuinely larger batch size, already covered, often works well, taking advantage of its more stable gradient estimates.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates how changing batch size affects the number of updates per epoch, using the exact same dataset size throughout.

code.content:
import numpy as np

dataset_size = 1000  # already covered as a factor in this topic

for batch_size in [16, 32, 64, 128, 256]:
    num_batches = int(np.ceil(dataset_size / batch_size))  # already covered as the last batch edge case in the previous topic
    print(f"Batch size {batch_size}: {num_batches} updates per epoch")

print("\nSmaller batch sizes produce more updates per epoch, already covered in this topic as the small batch size effect")
print("Larger batch sizes produce fewer updates per epoch, already covered in this topic as the large batch size effect")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the number of updates per epoch dropping sharply as batch size grows, exactly the tradeoff already covered in this topic between gradient stability and update frequency.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Batch Size is the hyperparameter controlling how many examples go into each batch.
Smaller batch sizes produce noisier gradients but more frequent updates per epoch.
Larger batch sizes produce more stable gradients but fewer updates per epoch.
Available hardware memory places a genuine, practical ceiling on batch size.
Smaller batch sizes can sometimes generalize better due to their added, noise-driven regularization.
Batch size and learning rate genuinely interact and are often tuned together.
Powers of 2 are a common convention, aligning well with modern hardware.
Batch size and dataset size together determine how many updates occur per epoch.
Next up: Iterations, the precise term for each individual weight update within an epoch.
